Remove an indexed drive or folder from the index: its files, folders, scans and what was recognised on it (signed manifests and the chain of custody stay). Nothing on it is touched. backdown forget [OPTIONS] <PATH> Copy
<PATH> The drive or folder as it was indexed ( backdown status lists them). Also takes the global options --db and --local .
Hash only what could be a duplicate: size, then a sample, then full SHA-256. What backdown hash does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown hash [OPTIONS] Copy
--jobs <JOBS> Readers per device; 1 suits spinning disks, raise it for SSDs. Default: 1 . --retry-errors Retry files that failed to read last time. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Hashes only what could be a duplicate: a file whose size no other file shares is never read. Then a sample (the first, middle and last 64 KiB) and, for files whose samples still match, the full SHA-256. Files on drives that aren't connected wait for them. See Hashes and proof .
backdown hash # an SSD: two readers per device backdown hash --jobs 2 # try the files that couldn't be read last time again backdown hash --retry-errors Copy
List duplicated content, largest reclaimable space first (runs hash first). What backdown dupes does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown dupes [OPTIONS] Copy

--min-size <MIN_SIZE> Ignore files smaller than this (e.g. 100K, 1M, 2G). Default: 1M . --limit <LIMIT> How many groups to list. Default: 20 . --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. --jobs <JOBS> Readers per device; 1 suits spinning disks, raise it for SSDs. Default: 1 . --retry-errors Retry files that failed to read last time. Also takes the global options --db and --local .
Hardlinks count once. Only fully hashed files are grouped, and dupes runs hash first.
backdown dupes backdown dupes --min-size 100M --limit 50 backdown dupes --json > dupes.json Copy
Is PATH safe to wipe? Every file needs a SHA-256-identical copy outside PATH (runs hash first). Exits 0 when safe, 2 when files must be copied first. backdown check [OPTIONS] <PATH> Copy
<PATH> The drive or folder to check. It must be there now (connected and mounted).

--list List the files that have no copy elsewhere (the largest 20,000). --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. --jobs <JOBS> Readers per device; 1 suits spinning disks, raise it for SSDs. Default: 1 . --retry-errors Retry files that failed to read last time. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Exits 0 when every file has a SHA-256-identical copy outside PATH ("SAFE TO WIPE"), and 2 when some files exist nowhere else or couldn't be read ("COPY FIRST"). Copies on drives that aren't connected still count: the verdict is about the index. --list lists the largest 20,000 such files. Empty files don't count against a drive.

backdown check /media/old-drive # every file that has no copy, largest first backdown check /media/old-drive --list # in a script: 0 = safe to wipe, 2 = copy first backdown check /media/old-drive && echo "safe to wipe" Copy
What "safe to wipe" means Free up a drive
Import the index the pre-Rust scripts wrote (bd-index.sh, bd-hash.py), so their crawling and hashing aren't repeated. backdown import-legacy [OPTIONS] <INDEX_DIR> Copy

--hashes <HASHES_DB> bd-hash.py's hashes.db: attach its SHA-256s to the files they belong to. --map <LEGACY=NOW> A drive mounted somewhere else now: LEGACY_PATH=PATH_NOW (repeatable; a legacy folder maps everything below it). --volume <NAME> Import only this volume, a folder name in INDEX_DIR (repeatable; default: all). --replace Replace what the index already holds for a root, or for roots nested with it. --dry-run Read everything and show what would be imported, writing nothing. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

The legacy index is the `index` folder the pre-Rust scripts wrote: <vol>/chunks.list bd-plan.py's crawl plan, one `R<TAB>dir` or `F<TAB>dir` per line; its first line, `F<TAB>/mount/point`, names the drive's root <vol>/chunks/<id>.tsv one chunk, from `find -printf '%s\t%T@\t%p\n'`: size, mtime (seconds.fraction) and the raw path; <id>.done marks it finished <vol>.tsv every finished chunk, merged (read when present and up to date) hashes.db bd-hash.py's table h(path, size, mtime, sha256) Each volume becomes a root with one finished scan, dated from its chunks. Chunks that never finished are left out and counted; the next `backdown index` adds their files. A hash attaches where the path, size and mtime (to the second) still match. Safe to run again: an interrupted import resumes, a finished one is left alone. Stop the daemon while importing. Afterwards `dupes` and `check` work straight away, and `backdown index <root>` with the drive mounted finds its files unchanged and keeps their hashes. Examples: backdown import-legacy ~/scripts/index --hashes ~/scripts/index/hashes.db --dry-run backdown import-legacy ~/scripts/index --hashes ~/scripts/index/hashes.db \ --map /media/olduser/Photos=/mnt/photos Copy
Every disk and partition on this machine: what's on it, and what BackDown can do with it (read-only; needs no root). backdown volumes [OPTIONS] Copy
--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Reads sysfs, udev and mountinfo on Linux, diskutil on macOS and the storage cmdlets on Windows. It never mounts or writes anything, says what BackDown can do with each partition (mountable, mounted, system, encrypted, part of a volume group, swap, empty), and marks the volumes an existing index covers.
Mounting drives read-only Troubleshooting: drives not showing up

How each drive is doing: SMART verdict, temperature, bad sectors, wear, and what changed since its first reading (read now, without root; kept in the index). Exits 2 when a connected drive is failing. backdown health [OPTIONS] Copy

--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. --machines The other machines' drives instead (Team), as each one's own BackDown last read them, fetched with its last sync: nothing is reached or read now. Exits 2 when a drive there is failing. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Reads each drive's own health reports (SMART) as you, without administrator rights: through udisks (and smartctl where your account may use it) on Linux, diskutil (and smartctl , if installed) on macOS, and the storage cmdlets on Windows, which share error counters only with an administrator. smartctl is asked not to wake a drive that has spun down. What can't be read is noted, with the command that would read it. Readings are kept in the index under the drive's serial number, so its history follows it from port to port. When the daemon runs (Linux and macOS), health has it read every drive now; it also reads them every six hours, when a drive appears and when an indexed drive comes back. No self-tests are run. Exits 2 when a connected drive is failing.
backdown health # in a script: 2 = a connected drive is failing backdown health --json > health.json Copy
Drive health Rescue a failing drive

Mount a partition read-only (one backdown volumes calls mountable), or attach a disk image read-only and mount what's on it; never read-write, and as you: udisks on Linux, diskutil and hdiutil on macOS (Windows attaches ISO, VHD and VHDX images). Without a target, lists what BackDown has mounted. backdown mount [OPTIONS] [TARGET] Copy
[TARGET] A partition (e.g. /dev/sdb1) or a disk image file. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Always read-only, and as you, through the system's own tools: udisksctl on Linux (it checks the mount really is read-only), diskutil and hdiutil on macOS, Mount-DiskImage on Windows. It refuses the running system's partitions, locked encrypted volumes, LVM and RAID members, swap and empty partitions. When the system wants an administrator's password, it shows the command to run instead. What it mounted is kept in mounts.json in your data folder.

# a partition `backdown volumes` calls mountable backdown mount /dev/sdb1 # a disk image: attached read-only, and what is on it mounted backdown mount /media/archive/Images/old-laptop.img # what BackDown has mounted backdown mount Copy
Mounting drives read-only A drive doesn't show up

Unmount a partition, or detach a disk image, that BackDown mounted (nothing else). What backdown unmount does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown unmount [OPTIONS] <TARGET> Copy
<TARGET> The partition or disk image, as backdown mount lists it. Also takes the global options --db and --local .
Only what backdown mount (or the browser's Mount read-only) mounted; detaching an image unmounts everything mounted from it.
Finished scans, oldest first. What backdown scans does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown scans [OPTIONS] Copy
--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .
Browse the index in your web browser: folders at any scan, versions, copies, file viewers. backdown serve [OPTIONS] Copy

--port <PORT> Port to listen on. Default: 8787 . --host <HOST> Also listen on this address (e.g. this computer's Tailscale IP) so other devices can look; from there BackDown only shows, and changes need this computer. 127.0.0.1 always listens. Default: 127.0.0.1 . --no-open Don't open a browser, just print the link. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

The browser listens on 127.0.0.1 and prints a private link with a one-time token. It only reads: copying, wiping, rescues and rescans need the background service ( backdown app , or backdown service install then backdown open ). --host ADDRESS also listens on that address, a Tailscale address such as 100.x.y.z say, and prints the link to use from your other devices. From anywhere but this computer, BackDown only shows what's there: nothing can be wiped, copied, rescued, mounted, opened or changed, and the link's token is still needed. A wildcard such as 0.0.0.0 listens on every address, 127.0.0.1 included.

backdown serve # another port, and just print the link backdown serve --port 8788 --no-open # also look from your other devices, at this computer's Tailscale address backdown serve --host 100.x.y.z Copy
Browse without restoring Look from your other devices
What's in the index (and what the daemon is doing). What backdown status does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown status [OPTIONS] Copy
--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .
Run in the background: rescan drives, hash, serve the web UI. Usually started by backdown service install rather than by hand. backdown daemon [OPTIONS] Copy

--port <PORT> Port for the web UI (0: any free one). Default: 8787 . Also read from $BACKDOWN_PORT . --host <HOST> Also listen on this address (e.g. this computer's Tailscale IP) so other devices can look; from there BackDown only shows, and changes need this computer. 127.0.0.1 always listens. Default: 127.0.0.1 . --rescan-every <RESCAN_EVERY> Rescan each drive this often (e.g. 12h, 1d; never to scan only on request or when a drive comes back). Default: as set in Settings (24h unless changed there). --system Machine-wide service: index in /var/lib/backdown, socket in /run/backdown, shared with the backdown group (set by the system unit). Also takes the global options --db and --local .

One job at a time (scan, hash, recognise, copy, mirror, wipe, tidy, mail merge), so the index has a single writer and each drive a single reader; rescues and syncs with other machines run beside them, and drive health is read every six hours. Every scan is followed by hashing, and recognition when something changed. Without --rescan-every , the interval is the one in Settings. --host works as for serve : the browser stays on 127.0.0.1 too, and from other devices it only shows and queues rescans (the link is http://ADDRESS:PORT/?t=TOKEN , with the token from ui.json in the data folder). On Linux and macOS the CLI talks to it through a socket in your runtime folder; on Windows, commands use the index directly.

# usually started by `backdown service install`; by hand: backdown daemon backdown daemon --rescan-every 12h # scan only when asked, or when a drive comes back backdown daemon --rescan-every never Copy
The background service Look from your other devices

Open the running daemon's web UI in your browser. What backdown open does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown open [OPTIONS] Copy Also takes the global options --db and --local .

The background service's browser token, for opening BackDown from a browser yourself (in a terminal, also the links with it in, including the one for other devices with --host). backdown token [OPTIONS] Copy
--links Print only the links, one per line. --qr Show the link for other devices as a QR code, for the BackDown phone app to scan. Also takes the global options --db and --local .
Tab completion for backdown's commands and options: print the script for a shell, or --install it for yours. backdown completions [OPTIONS] [SHELL] Copy
[SHELL] bash, zsh, fish, powershell or elvish (default: your shell, from $SHELL). One of bash , elvish , fish , powershell , zsh .
--install Put it where your shell picks it up, for you alone (bash, zsh, fish). Also takes the global options --db and --local .
Open BackDown in a window of its own, starting its background service first if need be (what the applications menu, Start menu and BackDown.app run). backdown app [OPTIONS] Copy

--no-window Only make sure the background service runs (for starting at login). --print Print the browser command instead of running it. --browser <BROWSER> A Chromium-family browser to use (default: Chrome, Chromium, Edge or Brave, whichever is installed; else your default browser). Also read from $BACKDOWN_BROWSER . Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Finds the running background service (yours, or on Linux the machine-wide one) or starts one: the installed service if there is one, else a daemon of its own, logging to daemon.log in your data folder. The window is Chrome, Chromium, Edge or Brave in app mode, with a profile of its own ( app-window in your data folder) that remembers its size and place; without one, a tab in your default browser. It opens with a one-time code, so the session token never goes on a command line. If BackDown's window is open already, it's brought forward.
backdown app # only make sure the background service runs (for starting at login) backdown app --no-window # a particular Chromium-family browser backdown app --browser /usr/bin/chromium Copy

Add BackDown to your applications menu, ~/Applications or the Start menu (or remove it). What backdown desktop does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown desktop [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Add BackDown to your applications: the menu and icons (Linux), ~/Applications/BackDown.app (macOS), or the Start menu (Windows). It opens backdown app . backdown desktop install [OPTIONS] Copy Options --autostart Also start BackDown's background service when you log in (on macOS, the login item backdown service install makes).
Remove what desktop install added (your index, settings and licence stay) backdown desktop uninstall [OPTIONS] Copy All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

Linux: io.backdown.BackDown.desktop and its icons in ~/.local/share (with --autostart , an autostart entry that runs backdown app --no-window ). macOS: ~/Applications/BackDown.app , a small bundle that runs this program (with --autostart , the LaunchAgent backdown service install makes). Windows: a Start menu entry (with --autostart , the scheduled task backdown service install makes). uninstall removes what install added and leaves the background service; backdown service uninstall removes that.
backdown desktop install # Linux and Windows: also start the background service when you log in backdown desktop install --autostart backdown desktop uninstall Copy
Is there a newer BackDown? Install it (verified against the release's signature and SHA-256 sums), from the network or from a folder carried over. backdown update [OPTIONS] Copy

--check Only say whether there is one (exits 10 when there is); with --from, only verify the folder and change nothing. --refresh Ask GitHub now instead of using today's answer. --rollback Put back the version the last update replaced. --channel <CHANNEL> stable or preview (default: as in Settings; previews while this is a preview). --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. --from <FOLDER> Install from FOLDER, without a network: it holds this system's release archive, SHA256SUMS.txt and SHA256SUMS.txt.sig, carried over from the release. --allow-unsigned With --from: go ahead without SHA256SUMS.txt.sig. The checksums then show only that the files arrived whole, not that they're BackDown's. --allow-older With --from: install it even if it isn't newer than this version. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Asks GitHub's public list of BackDown releases, only when you run it (or when Settings says to look once a day); the answer is kept for a day. Installing downloads this computer's archive and SHA256SUMS.txt , refuses unless the SHA-256 matches, checks the new program runs, keeps the old one in your data folder, swaps them and restarts the background service; if the new one doesn't start, the old one is put back. A copy installed by a package manager, an AppImage or Homebrew is updated that way instead, and it says so.

# is there a newer version? (exits 10 when there is) backdown update --check # download it, check it against SHA256SUMS.txt and install it backdown update # put back the version the last update replaced backdown update --rollback Copy
Run the daemon as a service (systemd on Linux, a login item on macOS, a task at logon on Windows): install, uninstall or check it. backdown service [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Install and start the daemon as a service for you (on Linux, machine-wide with --system) backdown service install [OPTIONS] Copy Options --system Machine-wide service running as the backdown user (needs sudo). --host <HOST> Also listen on this address (e.g. this computer's Tailscale IP) so other devices can look; from there BackDown only shows, and changes need this computer. 127.0.0.1 always listens. Default: 127.0.0.1 . --port <PORT> Port the service binds. Default: 8787 . --no-start Install but don't start it. --print Print the unit file instead of installing it.
Stop and remove the service (the index is kept) backdown service uninstall [OPTIONS] Copy Options --system
Is the service installed and running, and what is it doing? backdown service status [OPTIONS] Copy Options --system   All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

On Linux, a systemd user service that runs as you; with --system , a machine-wide service that runs as a backdown user that can read every file and write none, with no network beyond this machine (add people to the backdown group to let them use it). On macOS, a LaunchAgent ( ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.backdown.daemon.plist ) that runs while you're logged in; its log is in ~/Library/Logs/BackDown . On Windows, a scheduled task "BackDown" that starts it, without a window and with your normal rights, when you log on. --system is Linux-only. --host and --port go into the Linux unit (see daemon ); systemd keeps the machine-wide service off the network whatever they say, and on macOS and Windows they aren't passed to the service yet (run backdown daemon --host … instead). status exits 3 when the service isn't running. Uninstalling keeps the index.

backdown service install backdown service status # see what it would install first backdown service install --print # Linux: also look from your other devices over Tailscale backdown service install --host 100.x.y.z # machine-wide, on Linux (NAS, server) sudo backdown service install --system backdown service uninstall Copy
The background service The service on each system

What things are: mail stores, backups, phones, systems, repositories, libraries… with where they came from (reads small files like backup scripts on connected drives). backdown entities [OPTIONS] [PATHS]... Copy
[PATHS]... Only these drives (or the drives these paths are on).

--refresh Recognise again even if nothing was scanned since. --kind <KIND> Only this kind (mail-store, timemachine, ios-backup, git, photos, …). --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Kinds: mail-store , maildir , mdbox , thunderbird , nextcloud , nextcloud-server , timemachine , ios-backup , android-backup , system , home-mac , home-linux , home-windows , website , git , sql-dump , mongo-dump , sqlite-db , mysql-data , postgres-data , mongo-data , disk-image , photos , music , videos , export , downloads , recovery . Reading where things came from needs the drive connected: small files only (backup scripts, plists, git config, dump headers).
backdown entities backdown entities /media/old-drive --kind mail-store backdown entities --refresh --json > entities.json Copy
Recognised things and provenance People and databases
Who the things are about: everyone with a mailbox, a Nextcloud account, a home folder or a mail identity on any drive, with everything found of them. backdown people [OPTIONS] [Q] Copy
[Q] Only people whose name, address or paths contain this.
--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

A person is whoever has a mailbox in a mail server's store or a Maildir of their own, a Nextcloud account, a home folder, an identity in a Thunderbird profile, or is the contact a website's configuration names. The same address on two drives is one person: mailboxes, accounts and homes are gathered under one name, with how much there is of each. Nothing is read from inside messages or files; names come from paths, prefs.js , configuration.php and .env files.
backdown people # one person, by name, address or login backdown people alice backdown people --json > people.json Copy
The databases behind the dumps, data directories and sites on every drive: each one with every dump and live copy of it, and what used it. backdown databases [OPTIONS] [Q] Copy
[Q] Only databases whose name or paths contain this.
--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

A database is gathered from every dump of it ( mysqldump , phpMyAdmin, pg_dump , pg_dumpall , mongodump folders), its live data directory in a server backup (MySQL, MariaDB), SQLite files, and the sites and Nextcloud servers configured to use it ( wp-config.php , configuration.php , .env , config/config.php ). Dumps are named from their header when the drive is connected, else from the file name without its date. Compressed dumps say nothing in the header; the browser's viewer still streams them.
backdown databases # every copy of one database backdown databases shop backdown databases --json > databases.json Copy

Search inside things: mail by subject, sender and recipient; database dumps and SQLite files by table, column and, at full depth, the text in their rows. Reuses Dovecot's own index for mail headers and SQLite's full-text tables in place. backdown search [OPTIONS] [Q]... Copy
[Q]... Words to find (all of them; a phrase in quotes).

--kind <KIND> Only messages, tables or rows. --build Build or update the index first (the service does this after each scan). --force With --build: index everything again, not only drives scanned since. --depth <DEPTH> How much to index from now on: off, headers (the default) or full. --limit <LIMIT> Default: 50 . --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Names are found by the search box and find ; this searches inside things. Mail: every message's subject, sender, recipients and date, from Dovecot's own index ( dovecot.index.cache ) where a mailbox has one, else from the message files (headers only). Dumps and SQLite files: every table with its columns (and which columns the database indexed for full text), and at --depth full the text in the rows, text-typed columns only, up to 64 MiB a file. A SQLite full-text table (FTS3/4/5) is searched in place, through SQLite itself. The index keeps no copy of the text, only where each hit is. The service indexes after each recognition; --build does it now, skipping what is already indexed for the same scan.

backdown search invoice 2021 # a phrase, and only mail backdown search "garden work" --kind message # build the index now, then see what is indexed backdown search --build backdown search # index the text in rows too, from the next build on backdown search --depth full --build Copy

How much of each drive, folder and recognised thing already exists elsewhere, and where. What backdown overlaps does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown overlaps [OPTIONS] Copy
--min <MIN> Only list folders and things with at least this share elsewhere (e.g. 90%). Default: 0% . --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .
backdown overlaps # only what is at least 90% elsewhere backdown overlaps --min 90% Copy

The whole picture as a document: drives, what's on them, overlaps, duplicates, and which drives are safe to wipe. backdown report [OPTIONS] Copy
--html HTML instead of Markdown. -o , --output <OUTPUT> Write to this file instead of the terminal. --refresh Recognise every drive again first. Also takes the global options --db and --local .
The report reads the index as it is; run backdown hash (or check / dupes ) first so every duplicate is counted.
backdown report > report.md backdown report --html -o report.html Copy
Propose where everything on the old drives goes in one archive, and why (saved, so it can be applied). backdown plan [OPTIONS] Copy

--to <TO> The archive folder (on the drive that will keep everything). --from <FROM> Only file these drives (default: every indexed drive but the archive's). --schema <SCHEMA> Your own filing schema (start from backdown plan --print-schema ). --print-schema Print the built-in schema and exit. --merge-mail Merge copies of the same mailbox by Message-ID, instead of filing one and copying the other's extra files beside it. --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

A plan only proposes. The archive's own drive is never a source. Nothing is copied until backdown apply ID --go , and nothing is ever deleted. Mailboxes that are at least 90% the same as another of the same origin are filed once, with the other's extra files beside them; --merge-mail merges them by Message-ID instead.

backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive # only one drive backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive --from /media/old-drive # your own schema backdown plan --print-schema > schema.toml backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive --schema schema.toml Copy
File your old drives into one archive Merge mailboxes
Plans made so far. What backdown plans does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown plans [OPTIONS] Copy Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Apply a plan: show what it would do, or with --go copy, verify and journal every file (never deletes anything). backdown apply [OPTIONS] <PLAN> Copy
<PLAN> The plan's number, as backdown plan and backdown plans show it.
--go Actually copy (without it: a dry run). Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Every copy is written beside its destination under a temporary name, read back and compared before it takes its name. An existing destination is never overwritten: if it differs, it's reported as a conflict. Runs can be interrupted and resumed. Copies are clones or kernel copies where the drives allow, and are read back either way. A name the archive's drive would take for another, or can't hold, is copied under another name ( photo (2).jpg ) and journaled; extended attributes (macOS) and alternate data streams (Windows) are copied, and what couldn't be kept is listed. Exits 2 when there were conflicts or failures. With a daemon running, --go is handed to it, and it indexes the archive afterwards.
# what plan 3 would do (writes nothing) backdown apply 3 backdown apply 3 --go Copy

Get files back from a failing, formatted or emptied drive or card (only reads it). What backdown rescue does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown rescue [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Copy a failing drive or card into an image file: the good areas first, the bad ones later. Stop it any time (Ctrl+C) and run the same command again to carry on. A map beside the image (IMAGE.map, in GNU ddrescue's format) records what's been read. backdown rescue image [OPTIONS] <SOURCE> <IMAGE> Copy Arguments <SOURCE> The drive, partition or card (e.g. /dev/sdc), or an image file. <IMAGE> The image file to write, on another drive. Options --retries <RETRIES> Passes over unreadable sectors at the end. Default: 1 . --sector <SECTOR> Sector size to read unreadable areas in (512 or 4096; default: 4096 for drives on Linux, which reads them a page at a time anyway, else 512). --same-drive Allow the image on another partition of the same physical drive (not recommended for a failing drive; always allowed when the source is an image file).

Find photos, videos, documents and more by what's inside them, whatever the file system says (after files were deleted, or the drive was formatted), and save them sorted by kind. backdown rescue find [OPTIONS] --to <TO> <SOURCE> Copy Arguments <SOURCE> The drive, partition or card (e.g. /dev/sdc), or an image of one. Options --to <TO> The folder to save what's found in, on another drive. --only <ONLY> Only these kinds: groups (photos, videos, audio, documents, archives, other) or extensions (jpg, pdf, docx, …), comma-separated. --start <START> Where to start, in bytes (e.g. a lost partition's start from rescue partitions ). --end <END> Where to stop, in bytes.

Look for file systems the partition table doesn't list (after a drive was re-initialised, repartitioned, or shows as empty). Only reads. backdown rescue partitions [OPTIONS] <SOURCE> Copy Arguments <SOURCE> The drive or card (e.g. /dev/sdc), or an image of one. Options --deep Read every sector, not only where partitions usually start (as slow as copying it). --json Print what was found as JSON. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

Rescue never opens the index, so sudo backdown rescue … is safe to run; what it writes is handed back to the user who ran sudo. It only reads the source, and refuses to write the image or found files onto the drive being rescued (or, for an image, onto another partition of the same drive unless --same-drive ). Exits 2 when an image is incomplete or nothing was found. Browsing a found partition's files, recovering deleted files with their names (FAT, exFAT, NTFS) and copying files out are in the browser's Rescue view, not in this command.

backdown rescue image /dev/sdc /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img backdown rescue find /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img --to /media/archive/Rescue/sdc-files --only photos,documents backdown rescue partitions /dev/sdc # when your account can't read the drive sudo backdown rescue partitions /dev/sdc Copy
Rescue a failing drive Recover deleted files
Keep a folder (usually part of the archive) copied on another drive, and check the copy now and then. backdown mirror [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Start mirroring FOLDER into MIRROR (a folder on another drive) backdown mirror add [OPTIONS] <FOLDER> <MIRROR> Copy Arguments <FOLDER> The folder to keep copied, usually part of the archive. <MIRROR> Where the copy goes: a folder on another drive. Neither folder may be inside the other. Options --verify-every <VERIFY_EVERY> Re-read a sample of the mirror every this many days. Default: 30 .
Mirrors, and how they were when last synced and verified. backdown mirror list [OPTIONS] Copy

Copy what's new or changed (old copies are kept aside; nothing is deleted) backdown mirror sync [OPTIONS] [ID] Copy Arguments [ID] A mirror's number from backdown mirror list . Without it, every mirror.

Re-read files on the mirror and compare them with the source. backdown mirror verify [OPTIONS] [ID] Copy Arguments [ID] A mirror's number from backdown mirror list . Without it, every mirror. Options --percent <PERCENT> Share of the files to re-read (a different share each day). Default: 5 . --all Re-read every file.

Stop keeping a mirror (the copies stay where they are) backdown mirror remove [OPTIONS] <ID> Copy Arguments <ID> A mirror's number from backdown mirror list . All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

A sync never deletes: when a file changed, the mirror's old copy is moved to .backdown-versions/ in the mirror first, and files that exist only on the mirror are kept and counted. The daemon syncs each mirror daily and re-reads a sample on its schedule, whenever both drives are connected.
backdown mirror add /media/archive/Archive/Mail /media/backup/Mail backdown mirror list backdown mirror sync backdown mirror verify 1 --all backdown mirror remove 1 Copy

Free drives (or folders on them): delete only what has a verified copy elsewhere, moving what exists only here to --move-to first. Without --go, only shows what would happen. backdown wipe [OPTIONS] <PATHS>... Copy
<PATHS>... Drives, or folders on them, to free. Each must be on an indexed drive.

--move-to <MOVE_TO> Move what exists only in these paths here first (verified), instead of leaving it. --trust-index Don't re-read each file and its copy; trust the index's hashes (faster, a little less safe). Copies must still be there, as last scanned. --go Actually wipe. --confirm <CONFIRM> The drive name(s), as the dry run shows them. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Refuses the running system (outside home folders), a whole home folder, BackDown's own index, and anything not on an indexed drive. Each file is re-read before it's deleted, and so is its copy outside the selection; --trust-index checks only that the copy is still there as last scanned. Changed, new or unreadable files are left alone. Every deletion is journaled with its proof. Folders the wipe empties are removed (a drive's own top folder stays). A copy only on another machine ( backdown remote ) counts when that machine confirmed it within the proof window, and is read again there just before the deletion. --move-to keeps names as they are, and leaves a file in place if its extended attributes or alternate data streams couldn't be kept on the copy.

# what would happen (changes nothing) backdown wipe /media/old-drive # move what exists only there first, then wipe backdown wipe /media/old-drive --move-to /media/archive/Unsorted --go --confirm "old-drive" Copy
Free up a drive Several machines Principles
Your BackDown Pro licence: add a key, or show the one you have. What backdown license does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown license [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Check a licence key (offline) and keep it in your BackDown data folder. backdown license add [OPTIONS] <KEY> Copy Arguments <KEY> The key from your order confirmation (BD1.…), or - to read it from stdin.
Show the licence you have (exits 1 without one) backdown license show [OPTIONS] Copy
What's free, what's Pro, and what this copy may use. backdown license features [OPTIONS] Copy All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

The key is checked offline, on this machine, and kept in your BackDown data folder. show exits 1 when there's no licence. features lists which features are free and which need Pro; a pre-release version, such as a beta, unlocks everything.

backdown license add BD1.eyJ2Ijox… # or from a file or the clipboard, on stdin backdown license add - < licence.txt backdown license show # what is free, what is Pro, and what this copy may use backdown license features Copy
Other machines (a NAS, another computer) whose BackDown index is read over ssh, so copies there count for duplicates and wiping. backdown remote [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Add a machine whose BackDown index is read over ssh (with your keys; never a password) backdown remote add [OPTIONS] <NAME> <URL> Copy Arguments <NAME> What to call it, like nas or office-pc. <URL> ssh://[user@]host[:port] (a host alias from ~/.ssh/config works too). Options --remote-db <PATH> Its index there, if not its default (or the one its BackDown service uses). (The global --db is this machine's index). --backdown <PATH> Where backdown is there, if not on the PATH ssh sessions get. --no-test Don't try to reach it now.
The machines, their drives, and when they were last synced. backdown remote list [OPTIONS] Copy Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.
Forget a machine and what was cached about it (nothing there is touched) backdown remote remove [OPTIONS] <NAME> Copy Arguments <NAME> A machine's name from backdown remote list .

Fetch what changed in a machine's index (all of them without NAME); files there whose size matches a file here are hashed there, so copies can be proved. backdown remote sync [OPTIONS] [NAME] Copy Arguments [NAME] A machine's name from backdown remote list . Without it, every machine.
Try reaching a machine: ssh, BackDown there, its index. backdown remote test [OPTIONS] <NAME> Copy Arguments <NAME> A machine's name from backdown remote list .

Bring one of a machine's indexed files here: by its path there (as remote sync saw it) or its id in that machine's index. Read there only if it's still as scanned, and checked against its SHA-256 when that machine has one. backdown remote fetch [OPTIONS] <NAME> <WHAT> Copy Arguments <NAME>   <WHAT> The file's path on that machine, or its index id there. Options -o , --out <PATH> Where to save it (its own name in the current folder unless said).

How long a copy on another machine counts as proof after it was last confirmed there, and how often machines are synced. backdown remote settings [OPTIONS] Copy Options --proof-days <PROOF_DAYS> Days (1–90; 7 unless changed). --sync-hours <SYNC_HOURS> Hours between syncs (6 unless changed). All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

The other machine needs BackDown installed and an index. BackDown runs your system's ssh as you, with BatchMode=yes (never a password) and your known hosts, and starts backdown serve-stdio there, which only reads its index and hashes a file only when asked; nothing listens on the network, and no file's contents are sent. A copy there counts only by SHA-256, and only when confirmed there within the proof window (7 days unless changed). The background service syncs each machine every 6 hours. add , test and sync need Pro (unlocked in pre-release versions); list and remove don't. Windows machines can't be the other end yet.

backdown remote add nas ssh://you@nas.example.org # BackDown isn't on the PATH ssh sessions get there backdown remote add office ssh://office-pc --backdown /opt/backdown/backdown backdown remote test nas backdown remote sync backdown remote list # copies there count for 14 days after they were last confirmed there backdown remote settings --proof-days 14 backdown remote remove nas Copy

The pool: folders on the swarm's drives that drives are filed into, each file once. On the machine whose drive it's on: pool add FOLDER ; pool list shows every machine's. backdown pool [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Make a folder on one of this machine's drives part of the pool (it's created if need be) backdown pool add [OPTIONS] <PATH> Copy Arguments <PATH>   Options --reserve <SIZE|PCT> Room to keep free on its drive: a size (50G) or a share (5%); 5 % of the drive, at least 20 GB, unless said. --takes <PLACES> The top-level places it takes, like Mail,Media (unless said, anything).
Every pool folder of the swarm: this machine's, and the others' as they last said. backdown pool list [OPTIONS] Copy Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Change what a pool folder of this machine keeps free or takes. backdown pool set [OPTIONS] <FOLDER> Copy Arguments <FOLDER> Its path, or its number from pool list . Options --reserve <SIZE|PCT>   --takes <PLACES> The top-level places it takes (an empty value: anything).
Stop treating a folder of this machine as part of the pool (nothing in it is touched) backdown pool remove [OPTIONS] <FOLDER> Copy Arguments <FOLDER> Its path, or its number from pool list .

Where a drive's things would go in the pool: what's in it already (by content, on any machine), what's new, and which pool folder each thing goes into. Kept as a pool plan. backdown pool plan [OPTIONS] <DRIVE> Copy Arguments <DRIVE> The drive: its path as indexed here, or its folder name. Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Copy a drive into the pool as its plan says: each file read back there and compared by SHA-256; what's in the pool already, or not as the drive was last scanned, isn't sent. Stopped or interrupted, it carries on where it was. backdown pool send [OPTIONS] <PLAN> Copy Arguments <PLAN> The plan's number (backdown pool plans).

The pool plans made here, or one of them. backdown pool plans [OPTIONS] [ID] Copy Arguments [ID] A plan's number, to show it whole. Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

Every machine as one: each machine's drives, how full they are and what's indexed on them (this machine and the ones backdown remote reaches); swarm where NAME finds files on all. backdown swarm [OPTIONS] [COMMAND] Copy
--cached Don't ask the other machines now: show them as last synced. --json Print it as JSON.

Find files and folders by name on every machine: which machine, which drive, where. backdown swarm where [OPTIONS] <NAME>... Copy Arguments <NAME>... Words in the name (all of them must be in it). Options --limit <LIMIT> List this many at most. Default: 50 . --cached Don't ask the other machines now: search what was last synced of them. --json Print them as JSON. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

Tidy an archive: identical files in FOLDER share their storage, as hardlinks or clones. Both files are re-read first; every link is journaled. Without --go, only shows what would happen. backdown dedup [OPTIONS] <FOLDER> Copy
<FOLDER> The folder to tidy, usually the archive. Only files inside it, on the same drive, are linked.

--link <LINK> hard: one file with several names (any filesystem; editing one edits them all). clone: separate files sharing blocks until one changes (btrfs, XFS, APFS). Default: hard . --min-size <MIN_SIZE> Leave smaller files alone (e.g. 4K, 1M). Default: 4K . --dry-run Only show what would happen (the default). --go Link them. --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Only files the index has hashed and that are identical, on the same drive, inside FOLDER; files whose permissions, owner or extended attributes differ (and, for hardlinks, their modification time), or that also have names outside FOLDER, are left alone. Clones need btrfs, XFS or APFS. Each pair is read again first; every link is journaled, and running it again carries on. It refuses the running system, whole home folders and BackDown's index, and isn't available on Windows yet. Index the drive afterwards (the daemon does). Exits 2 when some files failed.

# what would be linked (changes nothing) backdown dedup /media/archive/Archive # on btrfs, XFS or APFS: separate files that share their blocks backdown dedup /media/archive/Archive --link clone --go Copy

Mailboxes: merge copies of one into a single Maildir, or export a Maildir folder as mbox. What backdown mail does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown mail [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Merge copies of the same mailbox taken at different times (Maildir, mbox files, a Thunderbird folder, or whole mail stores, mailbox by mailbox) into one Maildir: every message once by Message-ID, in the folder the newest copy has it in, flags combined. The sources are only read. backdown mail merge [OPTIONS] --to <TO> <SOURCES>... Copy Arguments <SOURCES>... The copies of the mailbox: Maildirs, mbox files, Thunderbird account folders, or whole mail stores (folders of Maildirs), in any order. They are only read. Options --to <TO> The merged Maildir: a new folder (running again carries on where it stopped). --dry-run Read everything and show what the merge would be, writing nothing. --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Export one Maildir folder (its own messages, not its subfolders) as an mbox file (mboxrd) backdown mail export [OPTIONS] --mbox <MBOX> <MAILDIR> Copy Arguments <MAILDIR> The Maildir folder to export (its own messages, not its subfolders). Options --mbox <MBOX> The mbox file to write (never overwritten). All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

Messages are matched by Message-ID and body (or, without a Message-ID, by headers and body); each lands in the folder the newest copy has it in, with read, replied and flagged marks combined. The destination must be new or empty; it becomes a Maildir++ mailbox. Every message is written, read back and journaled; an interrupted merge carries on when run again. Dovecot mdbox and sdbox aren't read yet. export never overwrites the mbox file. merge exits 2 when some messages failed.

# what the merge would be (writes nothing) backdown mail merge /media/old-drive/Mail/Inbox /media/laptop-2012/Mail/Inbox --to /media/archive/Mail/merged --dry-run backdown mail merge /media/old-drive/Mail/Inbox /media/laptop-2012/Mail/Inbox --to /media/archive/Mail/merged backdown mail export /media/archive/Mail/merged --mbox /media/archive/Mail/inbox.mbox Copy

The chain of custody: every copy, move, deletion, link and merge BackDown made, in a hash-chained log sealed with this installation's key. Export it as a signed bundle, verify one, or check the log in the index. backdown custody [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Write the chain of custody as a signed JSON bundle, sealing it first. With a filter, the events that don't match are elided: only their number, digest and hash are kept, so the chain still checks from end to end without showing their paths. backdown custody export [OPTIONS] --out <FILE> Copy Options --out <FILE> The file to write (never overwritten), or - for standard output. --since <DATE> Only show what was done from this day on (UTC): 2026-10-01, or 2026-10-01T14:30. --ref <JOB> Only show one job's events: plan:N, wipe:N, dedup:N, merge:N, rescue:N or mirror:N. --path <PREFIX> Only show what was done to files in this folder (or to this file).

Check an exported bundle: every event against its hash and the one before it, every seal's signature, that the seals reach the last event, and the bundle's own signature. Exits 1, saying what doesn't check out, if anything doesn't. backdown custody verify [OPTIONS] <FILE> Copy Arguments <FILE>   Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Check the chain of custody in the index the same way: whether anyone changed the database behind BackDown's back. Exits 1 if anything doesn't check out. backdown custody check [OPTIONS] Copy Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

Signed, tamper-evident manifests of what a drive held at a scan: sign one, check one (anyone can, here or on another computer), list the ones kept, show your signing key. backdown manifest [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Sign a manifest of DRIVE as of its latest finished scan: every file's path, size and hash in one Merkle root, signed with this installation's key and chained to the drive's previous manifest, and kept in the index. The document goes to the terminal unless --out names a file. backdown manifest create [OPTIONS] <DRIVE> Copy Arguments <DRIVE> The drive (an indexed folder), or a folder on it. Options --scan <SCAN> Attest this finished scan of the drive instead ( backdown scans lists them). --out <FILE> Write the signed document to this file (never overwritten). --list <FILE> Also write its listing, every file as a line of JSON, to this file: checking which files were signed needs it (never overwritten).

Check manifests: the signature; the chain, among several files or with the manifests this index keeps; with --list, that the listing is exactly what was signed. Exits 0 when it all checks, 2 when something doesn't. backdown manifest verify [OPTIONS] <FILE>... Copy Arguments <FILE>...   Options --list <FILE> The manifest's listing (with one manifest). --against-index Also compare it with the index now: what was added, removed or changed on the drive since (with one manifest). --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

The manifests this index keeps, oldest first (one drive's, or every drive's), and whether each drive's chain is whole. backdown manifest list [OPTIONS] [DRIVE] Copy Arguments [DRIVE] Only this drive (or the drive this folder is on). Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Write out a manifest this index keeps (by its number in manifest list ), and its listing, made again from the index's record of its scan. backdown manifest export [OPTIONS] <ID> Copy Arguments <ID>   Options --out <FILE> Write the document to this file instead of the terminal (never overwritten). --list <FILE> Write its listing to this file (never overwritten).

This installation's signing key: its fingerprint and public key, for whoever checks your manifests (made now if there's none yet) backdown manifest key [OPTIONS] Copy Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .
Tags: facts about content — person, place, kind, event, date. Create them and attach them to content, people or places. backdown tag [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Create a tag (or find the matching one), and optionally attach it to a target. backdown tag add [OPTIONS] --kind <KIND> --value <VALUE> Copy Options --kind <KIND> What it is about: owner, kind, location, country, city, place, airport, event, date, memory. --value <VALUE> Its value, e.g. "Hong Kong" or "HKG". --parent <PARENT> A parent tag id, for a hierarchy (a city under its country). --data <DATA> Extra data as JSON (coordinates, codes). --to <TARGET> Attach it to this target: content:<sha256hex>, subject:<key>, entity:<key> or path:<key>. --source <SOURCE> Where the tag came from. Default: user . --confidence <CONFIDENCE> How sure, 0..1. Default: 1 .
Remove a tag from a target. backdown tag rm [OPTIONS] --tag <TAG> --from <TARGET> Copy Options --tag <TAG> The tag id ( backdown tag list ). --from <TARGET> The target to remove it from.
List tags, optionally of one kind. backdown tag list [OPTIONS] Copy Options --kind <KIND>   --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Show the tags a target carries. backdown tag of [OPTIONS] <TARGET> Copy Arguments <TARGET> content:<sha256hex>, subject:<key>, entity:<key> or path:<key>. Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Read a photo or video's own metadata (EXIF / QuickTime) and attach date and location tags. backdown tag exif [OPTIONS] <PATHS>... Copy Arguments <PATHS>... The files to read, or folders: every indexed photo and video under them (each must be indexed; one backdown hash hasn't read is hashed now). Options --geo Also tag the country, region, city and nearest airport of each position, as tag geo does. --again In folders, read again what was read before (named files always are). --source <SOURCE> Where the derived tags are recorded as coming from. Default: exif .

Find content by where it was taken and what it's tagged with: everything within a distance of a place, carrying tags, taken between dates. backdown tag find [OPTIONS] Copy Options --near <PLACE> Around a place: an airport's code (HKG), a town or city (Paris, or "Paris, Texas"), or a position (22.3089,113.9146). --km <KM> How far from it, in km. Default: 120 . --tag <KIND=VALUE> A tag it must carry: KIND=VALUE (airport=HKG, country=Hong Kong, event=Boat show 2019) or a tag id from tag list . Repeat it for more; all must be there. --from <DATE> Taken on or after: YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD. --to <DATE> Taken on or before: YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD. --sort <SORT> nearest (the default around a place), newest (otherwise) or oldest. --limit <LIMIT> Show at most this many (0: all of them). Default: 0 . --paths Print only the path of every copy, one per line, for scripts ( | xargs … ). --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.

Derive country, region, city and nearest-airport tags from the location tags already on content (attach those first with tag exif ). Offline, from embedded reference data. backdown tag geo [OPTIONS] [TARGETS]... Copy Arguments [TARGETS]... Limit to these content items (content:<sha256hex>); with none, every located item. Options --source <SOURCE> Where the derived tags are recorded as coming from. Default: geo . --about Print the embedded dataset sizes and data attribution, then exit. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

# read the dates and positions of every indexed photo and video under a folder, and name their places backdown tag exif ~/Pictures --geo # everything within 120 km of Hong Kong's airport, nearest first backdown tag find --near HKG # a town (the most populous of that name, or say which), closer in, in one year backdown tag find --near "Paris, France" --km 20 --from 2019 --to 2019 # by tags: all of them must be there backdown tag find --tag country="Hong Kong" --tag event="Boat show 2019" # just the paths, for other tools backdown tag find --near 22.3089,113.9146 --km 5 --paths | xargs -d '\n' ls -l backdown tag add --kind event --value "Boat show 2019" --to content:<sha256> Copy

Flags: a decision about an item — canonical, duplicate, keep, drop, reviewed. What backdown flag does, its options and examples, from the built-in help. backdown flag [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Copy

Set a flag on an item. backdown flag set [OPTIONS] <TARGET> <STATE> Copy Arguments <TARGET> content:<sha256hex>, subject:<key>, entity:<key> or path:<key>. <STATE> canonical | duplicate | keep | drop | reviewed | owner-confirmed | mine | not-mine. Options --canonical <TARGET> For a duplicate: the canonical copy's target. --by <BY> Who decided. Default: user . --note <NOTE>
Clear a flag from an item. backdown flag clear [OPTIONS] <TARGET> <STATE> Copy Arguments <TARGET>   <STATE>
Show an item's flags. backdown flag of [OPTIONS] <TARGET> Copy Arguments <TARGET>   Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

Add a relationship edge: SRC REL DST, each node as type:key. backdown edge add [OPTIONS] <SRC> <REL> <DST> Copy Arguments <SRC>   <REL>   <DST>   Options --data <DATA>
Edges out of a node. backdown edge from [OPTIONS] <SRC> Copy Arguments <SRC>   Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.
Edges into a node. backdown edge to [OPTIONS] <DST> Copy Arguments <DST>   Options --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. All of them also take the global options --db and --local .

What changed in each release of BackDown, newest first (1.0.0-beta.12 is the latest), with the installers and checksums of each on GitHub. Every release of BackDown, newest first. The latest is 1.0.0-beta.12 ; the Download page always has the current one, and backdown update installs it, checking the release's signature first. Each page is that release's notes as published on GitHub .

The twelfth beta of BackDown 1.0: the rest of the write-ahead log fix. If you're on beta.8 or earlier, this is the one to take. Released 2026-11-14 · downloads and checksums on GitHub · Download page The twelfth beta of BackDown 1.0: the rest of the write-ahead log fix. If you're on beta.8 or earlier, this is the one to take. beta.9 taught BackDown to reclaim the index's write-ahead log as it goes, which stops it growing while a long scan runs beside readers. This beta closes the other ways it could still grow. When a scan found that a great many files had gone — a drive emptied, a big folder moved away — it closed them all in one statement inside one transaction, and on a large index that one transaction could write more log than the index itself holds (47 GB, on 8 November). Forgetting a machine's cached files, or one of its drives, did the same over millions of rows. Both now go 20,000 rows at a time, the log reclaimed between batches. Syncing another machine's index is hours of pages, and nothing reclaimed the log between them: a status count or a report that outlasted a page held the log's growth for as long as it ran, and the file then kept that size for the rest of the sync (1 GB on a 17-million-file drive). Each page's commit reclaims it now, and so does the end of every background job. Reclaiming also no longer waits out the writer's 30-second patience behind a slow reader, and opening the index writes nothing when nothing has changed.

Platform Installer Command line Linux x86-64 backdown-io_1.0.0-beta.12_amd64.deb (Debian, Ubuntu) or .AppImage backdown-v1.0.0-beta.12-linux-x86_64.tar.gz (static) Linux ARM64 backdown-io_1.0.0-beta.12_arm64.deb or .AppImage backdown-v1.0.0-beta.12-linux-arm64.tar.gz (static) macOS (Apple silicon + Intel) BackDown-1.0.0-beta.12.dmg backdown-v1.0.0-beta.12-macos-universal.tar.gz Windows builds are paused for this beta while the port is finished; follow it at https://github.com/BuenGenio/BackDown/issues/94 . This release is signed. SHA256SUMS.txt.sig is an Ed25519 signature of SHA256SUMS.txt by BackDown's release key, and backdown update checks it before installing anything. To check by hand, see Air-gapped computers . The installers and apps themselves still aren't signed by Apple. On macOS, right-click the app and choose Open the first time (for the command-line binary: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine backdown ).

A scan that finds many files gone closes them 20,000 at a time, each batch committed and the write-ahead log reclaimed, instead of one statement over the whole drive: closing 200,000 files now leaves an 8 KB log where it left 44 MB, and the growth no longer scales with the index. Forgetting a machine's cached files ( backdown remote remove , or a drive of it that was re-indexed from scratch) goes the same way: millions of rows, a batch at a time. Syncing another machine reclaims the log after every page of files it fetches, and every background job reclaims it when it finishes: a reader that outlasts a page no longer sets the log's size for the rest of the sync (60,000 files in 12 pages: 7 MB before, under 2 MB now). Reclaiming the log waits a quarter of a second for readers, not the writer's 30 seconds: a slow reader no longer stalls a scan at every batch, nor every command as it opens the index. Opening the index writes nothing when the schema is already current, so commands that only read never take the writer's lock.

Released 2026-11-09 · downloads and checksums on GitHub · Download page The ninth beta of BackDown 1.0: a reliability fix, nothing else. A long index run — including the one-time names index that beta.7/beta.8 build the first time they open a big index — committed its work in safely bounded batches, but never reclaimed the space those batches left behind in the index's write-ahead log. On an idle reader (even one just sitting on an old snapshot) and a big enough drive, that log could grow without bound instead of shrinking back down: on one 27-million-file index it grew past 47 GB and filled the disk. BackDown now reclaims that space as it goes — after every batch, when the index opens, and between jobs — so upgrading from any earlier beta, even on a very large index, no longer carries that risk.

Tags, flags and links Tags say what something is about: its owner, kind, place, country, city, airport, event, date. backdown tag add --kind city --value "Hong Kong" --to TARGET , tag rm , tag list , tag of TARGET . Tags can nest (a city under its country). A tag on a file's content ( content:<sha256> ) is on every copy of that file, on any drive, and stays when copies are moved or deduplicated. Tags can also go on a person or database ( subject: , entity: ) or a path ( path: ). Flags record decisions: canonical , duplicate (of which copy), keep , drop , reviewed , mine , not-mine and others. backdown flag set|clear|of . Links between any two things: backdown edge add SRC REL DST , edge from , edge to . --json on everything that reads. Each tag and flag remembers where it came from and when. A photo's date and place backdown tag exif FILES reads the date and GPS position a photo or video recorded (JPEG, HEIC, TIFF, MOV, MP4) and tags its content with the year, the date under it, and the location. The files need to be indexed; one BackDown hasn't hashed yet (a file no other file matches in size never is) is hashed there and then. backdown tag geo turns those locations into country, region, city and nearest airport (within 120 km), offline, from place data built into BackDown. Nothing is sent anywhere. The further a photo is from the nearest town, the lower the confidence recorded with the tag. backdown tag geo --about shows the data it uses and where it comes from: GeoNames (CC BY 4.0) and OurAirports (public domain). Scans refuse the wrong drive After a reboot on a user's server, a drive came up at a different mount point, and other software had already made a few folders at its usual one. BackDown's next scan saw those folders instead of the drive and marked almost 16 million files as gone; getting them back would have meant hashing terabytes again. Scans now stop before recording anything when: another drive is where the scanned one was : the folder is now on a different disk (by serial or file system UUID) from the last scan. The message names both and says what to do: mount the drive there, or backdown index --allow-other-drive for a new drive in the old one's place, or backdown forget and index it afresh. no files are found where the last scan found some ( --allow-empty overrides, as before); the folder itself can't be read , even with --allow-empty . A folder lower down that can't be read keeps its files as they were, rather than counting them as deleted. A refused scan leaves no trace in the history. Under the hood The licence list shipped with every download covers the new components, and credits the place data.

The swarm, and the pool Every machine as one. The machines backdown remote reaches, plus this one, show up together: each machine's drives as bars of used and free space, what's indexed on them, their health, drives that aren't connected and the machine they were last scanned on, and the totals. backdown swarm , and the browser's Swarm view. A drive is known by its serial and volume UUID, so one that moves between machines is the same drive. Where is it. backdown swarm where NAME and the Swarm view's search ask every machine at once, live where it can be reached and from what was synced where it can't: machine, drive, path. The pool. backdown pool add FOLDER [--reserve 50G] [--takes Mail,Media] makes a folder on one of a machine's drives part of a shared, filed archive; the other machines learn of it at their next sync. The pool keeps one copy of each file. A drive into the pool. backdown pool plan DRIVE says, thing by thing, what's in the pool already (by SHA-256, on any machine), what's new, and which pool folder each thing goes into and why; you move or leave out what you like; backdown pool send copies it, verified by the hash read back there, resumable, and then offers to free the drive. It works for a drive plugged into another machine too, from here: the plan is made and carried out there, by that machine's own BackDown. Copies between machines stream over ssh to backdown swarm-stdio , which writes only inside that machine's own pool folders. Several machines is free now, as the swarm is built on it. Syncing a big drive from another machine no longer times out; what to ask it to read is found in seconds rather than a minute a batch. Files from whichever machine holds them A file on another machine's page has Preview , Download a copy and Open , and backdown remote fetch nas PATH -o DIR saves one here from the terminal, checked against the hash that machine has. The other machine reads a file only if it's still exactly as its index scanned it. Files up to 256 MB come through a small cache here so a second look costs nothing; bigger ones stream the part asked for. Indexing stays each machine's own business: this brings one file you asked for, never a drive. People and databases More kinds of thing recognised : mongodump folders, SQLite files, and the data directories of MySQL/MariaDB, PostgreSQL and MongoDB servers; dump headers from phpMyAdmin, pg_dump, pg_dumpall and SQLite's .dump ; and what a website's or Nextcloud server's configuration says ( wp-config.php , Joomla, Laravel .env , Nextcloud config.php ): the database behind it, where it was served, who to contact. People ( backdown people , What's here > People): everyone with a mailbox in a mail store, a Nextcloud account, a home folder, a Thunderbird identity or named as a site's contact, gathered across drives into one person with what there is of them. The same address, or the same login on the same host, is one person; a name alone never merges two. Databases ( backdown databases , What's here > Databases): each database with every dump of it, its live data, its SQLite file, and the sites and servers configured to use it, under one name per engine family. Search inside mail and databases backdown search WORDS and the search box's Inside scope find messages by subject, sender and recipient, and dumps and SQLite files by table, column and (at full depth) the text in their rows. Indexes already on the drives are reused : Dovecot's own dovecot.index.cache is read for the headers of a whole mailbox without opening a message; SQLite full-text tables (FTS3/4/5) are searched in place through SQLite itself; a dump's FULLTEXT KEY columns are listed with the table. Depth is a setting ( off , headers , full ); the service indexes after each recognition, only drives scanned since. The index keeps no copy of the text, only where each hit is. The app and the browser BackDown for Android and iOS (Flutter): the browser's views on a phone, over the same connection. backdown token --qr shows the link for other devices as a QR code. Remove a drive from the index , from its page or backdown forget , scans and all; and a scan in progress can be stopped. Settings has real tabs, one section at a time. backdown open , token and app say whose daemon is on the port instead of "none is running". The Machines page keeps each drive's cached and hashed counts across syncs. A live UI preview for development ( scripts/preview-ui.py ). The store Pro, Team and Forensic pre-orders, each with its own licence; licences name their edition and count Forensic seats as sites. Nothing is switched on in this release: everything stays unlocked during the beta. Fixes and under the hood Hashing: a file no longer inherits another file's SHA-256 through a reused inode number. The spreadsheet viewer moved off a zip release with a known vulnerability (zip 9, calamine 0.37). One transaction type that rolls back when dropped, so a failed job can't leave one open; one clock, one hex decoder, one mount-table reader, one mbox rule instead of several copies. The viewers (archives, disk images, mail, spreadsheets, slides, SQL dumps) are a crate of their own, and the recogniser, rescue carving, update, mailbox and mail-merge modules are split into files by stage. The pre-Rust scripts moved to legacy/ , with a README.

Signed manifests (Forensic): backdown manifest create signs a statement of exactly what a drive held at a scan, every file's path, size and SHA-256 combined into one Merkle root, each chained to the drive's previous one. Anyone can check one with backdown manifest verify , or without BackDown from the algorithm in the guide . Scheduled attestations (Team): Settings > Attestations has the service sign a manifest of each drive after every scan, daily or weekly. Chain of custody (Forensic): every copy, move, deletion, link and merge BackDown makes goes into a hash-chained log, sealed with this installation's key. backdown custody export exports it, whole or for one job (other events are elided, the chain still verifies), verify checks a bundle anywhere, and check finds edits made to the index directly. The log is kept in every edition; it starts with this release. Air-gapped computers (Forensic): backdown update --from FOLDER installs a release carried over on a drive, its signature checked first and no network used. Checking such a folder ( --from … --check ) is free. Drive health from your other machines (Team): the machines you've added report their drives' health with each sync, shown in Activity and backdown health --machines , with a notification when one gets worse. Duplicates, reworked : one entry per set of identical files that opens to its copies, or grouped by the folders they're in, with the filter bar applied, thumbnails, and ticks that hand copies to Free up. The second beta of BackDown 1.0: faster on very large indexes, easier to reach from your other devices, and Tab completion in the terminal. Released 2026-10-01 · downloads and checksums on GitHub · Download page The second beta of BackDown 1.0: faster on very large indexes, easier to reach from your other devices, and Tab completion in the terminal.

Platform Installer Command line Linux x86-64 backdown-io_1.0.0-beta.2_amd64.deb (Debian, Ubuntu) or .AppImage backdown-v1.0.0-beta.2-linux-x86_64.tar.gz (static) Linux ARM64 backdown-io_1.0.0-beta.2_arm64.deb or .AppImage backdown-v1.0.0-beta.2-linux-arm64.tar.gz (static) macOS (Apple silicon + Intel) BackDown-1.0.0-beta.2.dmg backdown-v1.0.0-beta.2-macos-universal.tar.gz Windows x86-64 BackDown-1.0.0-beta.2-x64.msi (no administrator rights needed) backdown-v1.0.0-beta.2-windows-x86_64.zip The Linux package is now called backdown-io . Debian and Ubuntu have an unrelated duplicate remover called backdown , and apt could have offered it as an "upgrade" of ours. sudo apt install ./backdown-io_*.deb replaces the backdown package of beta.1 (and that other program, since both install /usr/bin/backdown ). If a terminal ever suggests sudo apt install backdown , that's the other one. These builds aren't signed yet. On macOS, right-click the app and choose Open the first time (for the command-line binary: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine backdown ). On Windows, SmartScreen may ask you to confirm once. Verify any download against SHA256SUMS.txt .

Large indexes : the duplicates report answers in seconds rather than minutes on an index of 17 million files, from a covering index the background service builds once after the upgrade ("Prepare the duplicates index" in Activity). The app's first screen no longer waits for the index's totals, which are now counted in one pass and kept, and backdown service status answers at once. Look from your other devices : --host now answers to the computer's full Tailscale name ( name.tailnet-….ts.net ) as well as its address and short name; BACKDOWN_HOST_NAMES allows others. From other devices BackDown still only shows what's there. backdown token : the background service's browser token, and with --links the links with it in, for this computer and for your other devices. Tab completion : backdown completions --install for bash, zsh or fish; the .deb sets it up for everyone. Servers : backdown service install explains what to do instead of half-installing when it's run with sudo or without a login session.

Built locally, not by CI. Every test passed on Linux; the macOS and Windows builds are checked but haven't yet run on those systems. The first beta of BackDown 1.0: every feature planned for 1.0 is in. It finds out what's on your drives, what's duplicated, where it came from and which drives are safe to free, then helps you file everything into one archive, free the old drives and rescue failing ones. Released 2026-09-29 · downloads and checksums on GitHub · Download page The first beta of BackDown 1.0: every feature planned for 1.0 is in. It finds out what's on your drives, what's duplicated, where it came from and which drives are safe to free, then helps you file everything into one archive, free the old drives and rescue failing ones. It runs locally and makes no network requests unless you ask.

Platform Installer Command line Linux x86-64 .deb (Debian, Ubuntu) or .AppImage backdown-v1.0.0-beta.1-linux-x86_64.tar.gz (static) Linux ARM64 .deb or .AppImage backdown-v1.0.0-beta.1-linux-arm64.tar.gz (static) macOS (Apple silicon + Intel) BackDown-1.0.0-beta.1.dmg backdown-v1.0.0-beta.1-macos-universal.tar.gz Windows x86-64 BackDown-1.0.0-beta.1-x64.msi (no administrator rights needed) backdown-v1.0.0-beta.1-windows-x86_64.zip Open BackDown from your applications menu, or run backdown app : it starts BackDown in the background and opens it in its own window. These builds aren't signed yet. On macOS, right-click the app and choose Open the first time (for the command-line binary: xattr -d com.apple.quarantine backdown ). On Windows, SmartScreen may ask you to confirm once. Verify any download against SHA256SUMS.txt .

The app : backdown app in its own window, desktop integration, installers for all three systems, a Settings view, and backdown update (checksum-verified, with rollback). Update checks are off unless you turn them on. Drive health : SMART readings without administrator rights, trends, warnings before a drive dies, desktop notifications, and "Copy it now" into Rescue. Rescans in seconds : from the drive's own change log (the USN journal on Windows, FSEvents on macOS) and by reading NTFS's file table directly, with a full scan whenever anything can't be vouched for. Free in every edition. Free up drives : tick what to wipe; a file is deleted only when an identical copy elsewhere is read back first; what exists only there is moved to a folder you choose. Rescue : copy a failing drive ddrescue-style, find deleted photos and documents by their content, find lost partitions, browse a found partition, and undelete files with their original names on FAT, exFAT and NTFS. Browse without restoring : mailboxes as threaded conversations, SQL dumps as schemas, the files inside disk images (FAT, exFAT, ext, NTFS), and search across every drive at once. Where things came from, and when : iPhone backups, Time Machine (including APFS), SQL dumps and backup scripts. Several machines (Pro, free during the beta): add a NAS or another computer over SSH; copies there count, carefully, as proof. Look from your other devices : backdown serve --host ADDRESS (and daemon , service install ) also listens on, say, your Tailscale address. From there BackDown only shows what's there; freeing up, copying, rescue and settings stay with the computer it runs on. The archive : fast verified copies, merging mailbox snapshots by Message-ID, and opt-in dedup inside the archive. macOS and Windows : case- and Unicode-safe names, long paths, NTFS alternate data streams, extended attributes, reading as a backup operator when elevated, and online-only files (OneDrive, iCloud) left alone rather than downloaded.
